To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the formation of Jovian planets is accompanied by the formation of a massive, dense and hot gaseous envelope, (2) this envelope is not hydrostatically stable and is therefore subject to vigorous dynamical activity, (3) the dynamical activity in the envelope can produce shocks that have temperatures and densities similar to the conditions required to form chondrule-like materials, and (4) the shocks can form chondrule analogs and annealed silicates, and

(1) a 3D hydrodynamical model of the envelope of a forming Jovian planet can produce shocks that are sufficiently energetic to form chondrule-sized silicates and (2) the spatial distribution of these shocks in the envelope is consistent with the spatial distribution of chondrules and silicate inclusions observed in meteorites.
the dynamical activity in the envelope of the forming Jovian planet, Jupiter, may be the source of the nebular shocks thought to be the origin of chondrules and annealed silicates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the formation of chondrules and the annealed silicates found in chondritic meteorites.
the formation of planets and planetesimals, and the origin of the chondritic components of the solar system, and we are currently working on a number of projects in these areas.
the origin of chondrules, the most important component of chondritic meteorites.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the formation of chondrules and the formation of Jupiter are intimately related.
the chondrules are formed by a combination of shock and radiation heating, but the exact details are not yet fully worked out.
the chondrule-formers are not the result of a nebular shock but are the product of a shock in a Jovian planet's envelope.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the envelope is a dynamical environment that is a potential source for shock heating of the nebula and that it may be a source of shock heating that is more effective and widespread than that provided by the protosun.

the formation of Jovian planets in the solar nebular is an inherently 3D process, and the resulting dynamical activity of the planet-forming envelope is capable of producing the thermal and dynamic conditions necessary to form annealed silicates.
the envelope of a forming Jupiter is a viable source of chondrule-formative shocks in the solar protoplanetary disk.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the dynamical activity associated with the formation of Jupiter and the other giant planets in the solar nebular is likely responsible for the production and annealing of chondrules and the formation of other annealed silicate materials in the solar nebulous.
the formation of Jovian planets is an inherently dynamic process, which may have significant implications for planet formation and the early evolution of our solar system.
the formation of chondrules is intimately connected with the formation of gas giant planets.
